output.query: aneurysmal SAH management Hunt-Hess WFNS Fisher coiling clipping

results.finding: The Hunt and Hess scale grades the clinical severity of aneurysmal SAH from I to V and correlates with surgical risk and outcome.
The amount and distribution of subarachnoid blood on the admission CT predicts later vasospasm.
Surgical or endovascular treatment of the ruptured aneurysm should be performed as early as feasible, preferably within 24 hours of onset; early enteral nimodipine improves outcome.
In ruptured aneurysms suitable for both techniques, endovascular coiling gave a higher rate of independent survival at one year than neurosurgical clipping.

output.summary: Clinical grade (Hunt and Hess, WFNS) and CT blood burden (Fisher) stratify outcome and vasospasm risk. Guidelines recommend securing the ruptured aneurysm as early as feasible, preferably within 24 hours, and early enteral nimodipine. Where an aneurysm suits both techniques, coiling was associated with better one-year independent survival than clipping.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Fisher grade 3 SAH in the basal cisterns, both Sylvian fissures and the anterior interhemispheric fissure; no intraventricular blood or hydrocephalus
action_criteria.label: Obtain an urgent noncontrast head CT as the mandatory first-line study for suspected aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage
action_criteria.rationale: Non-contrast head CT is the first study in suspected SAH: it shows subarachnoid blood and its distribution, intraventricular blood and hydrocephalus.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Troponin I 2.8 ng/mL, BNP 486, glucose 188, WBC 14.8; platelets, potassium, magnesium and coagulation normal
action_criteria.label: Obtain the condition-specific baseline blood work: CBC, metabolic panel and coagulation studies
action_criteria.rationale: Blood count, electrolytes (sodium, potassium, magnesium), renal function and coagulation are needed before securing or CSF diversion and for sodium and QTc management.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus tachycardia 114 with deep symmetric T-wave inversions V1-V5 without ST elevation; QTc 532 ms
action_criteria.label: Obtain 12-lead ECG to evaluate for neurogenic stress changes and exclude concurrent primary cardiac event
action_criteria.rationale: Neurogenic ECG changes are common in SAH; the ECG screens for a primary cardiac event and sets the QTc baseline.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AComA aneurysm 7.8 x 6.4 mm with an irregular multilobulated dome; no other aneurysm; no dissection
action_criteria.label: After the noncontrast CT, obtain a separate head-and-neck CT angiogram to localize the culprit aneurysm and plan treatment; CTA does not replace the index NCCT
action_criteria.rationale: CTA localizes the ruptured aneurysm and defines the anatomy that decides coiling or clipping; it is a separate acquisition after the NCCT.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AComA aneurysm 7.9 x 6.4 mm confirmed, neck 3.4 mm, dome-to-neck ratio 2.3, right A2 origin partly incorporated into the neck
action_criteria.label: Obtain catheter cerebral angiography with 3D rotational imaging to confirm the ruptured aneurysm and define its anatomy before securing
action_criteria.rationale: Catheter angiography with 3D rotational imaging confirms the ruptured aneurysm and its relation to branch vessels before securing, and is the reference test when CTA is negative.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Aspirin with clopidogrel: irreversible platelet inhibition raising rebleeding and procedural risk; stent thrombosis risk lower 2 years after stenting; platelet transfusion only before a neurosurgical procedure
action_criteria.label: Check the dual antiplatelet therapy (with the extra EMS aspirin dose) and the home antihypertensives against nimodipine before securing
action_criteria.rationale: Aspirin, clopidogrel and an extra 325 mg aspirin change the bleeding risk of the unsecured aneurysm and of its securing; the stent makes stopping them a joint decision with cardiology.

action_criteria.rationale: Troponin elevation with neurogenic ECG changes warrants echocardiography for stress cardiomyopathy, which also informs the anesthetic plan.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture before non-contrast CT in suspected SAH.
Do not perform lumbar puncture when CT already confirms SAH with mass effect, intraventricular hemorrhage, or hydrocephalus — herniation risk.
Do not start aspirin or other antiplatelet agents before the aneurysm is secured — increases rebleeding risk.
Do not inject the contents of nimodipine capsules intravenously or by any other parenteral route (risk of cardiovascular collapse); give nimodipine enterally.
Do not give NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, ketorolac) for headache control before aneurysm securing — antiplatelet effect raises rebleeding risk.
Do not pursue cardiac catheterization for neurogenic troponin elevation without strong primary-ACS evidence — delays aneurysm treatment.
Do not leave severe hypertension untreated before the aneurysm is secured, and do not lower blood pressure to the point of hypotension.
required_recommendations: Initiate non-contrast CT head as the first diagnostic step in suspected SAH; do not delay for other workup.
Obtain CT angiography of the head and neck immediately after positive non-contrast CT to characterize the aneurysm.

Start enteral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours (orally or by nasogastric tube) as soon as aneurysmal SAH is confirmed and continue for 21 days; if it causes hypotension, give 30 mg every 2 hours rather than stopping it [Hoh_2023].

Arrange urgent joint neurosurgical and neurointerventional review and secure the ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm by endovascular coiling or microsurgical clipping as early as feasible, preferably within 24 hours of onset [Hoh_2023]; the technique is chosen jointly from the aneurysm anatomy and the patient's condition.
Admit to a neurocritical care unit at a centre with neurosurgical and neurointerventional capability, with hourly neurological checks and continuous cardiac monitoring.

Lower blood pressure now with a short-acting titratable intravenous agent (nicardipine or clevidipine infusion) until the aneurysm is secured, avoiding hypotension; the 2023 guideline sets no numeric target [Hoh_2023] and systolic pressure below 160 mmHg is the commonly used target [Connolly_2012].

Continue metoprolol succinate (post-MI therapy) unless bradycardia or hypotension develops, without stopping it abruptly; withhold lisinopril during the acute phase and resume once stable; continue atorvastatin.
Hold aspirin and clopidogrel (including the extra EMS dose); agree with cardiology given the 2-year-old coronary stent, and consider platelet transfusion only if an EVD or open surgery is required.

QTc 532 ms with potassium 3.6 mmol/L: replete potassium to at least 4.0 mmol/L and magnesium to at least 2.0 mg/dL, avoid adding QT-prolonging drugs (for example ondansetron or haloperidol), and keep continuous ECG monitoring with daily QTc [Drew_2010].

LVEF 30% from stress cardiomyopathy, with moderate mitral regurgitation: involve cardiology and neuroanesthesia before the securing procedure (hemodynamic plan, invasive arterial monitoring) and repeat echocardiography to document recovery.
Monitor serum sodium closely for cerebral salt wasting / SIADH and avoid hypotonic fluids.

Monitor for delayed cerebral ischemia from day 3 to day 14 with frequent neurological examinations, with transcranial Doppler surveillance as a reasonable adjunct; maintain euvolemia and do not use prophylactic hypervolemia [Hoh_2023].

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is not part of standard SAH workup; reserve for evaluation of unexplained altered mental status suggesting non-convulsive status epilepticus.
EMG/NCS has no role in acute SAH evaluation or management.
Sleep study is irrelevant to acute SAH workup.

accepted: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage from AComA aneurysm with neurogenic Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, complicated by dual antiplatelet therapy

differential.key_features: Chest pain, troponin I 2.8 ng/mL and T-wave inversions in a man with prior STEMI overlap; symmetric T-wave inversions without ST elevation or Q waves, and apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis beyond one coronary territory, favor stress cardiomyopathy from the SAH.

Thunderclap onset and the exertional trigger overlap with SAH; RCVS gives convexity SAH and segmental vasoconstriction, whereas this case shows basal-cistern blood and a saccular AComA aneurysm on CTA.
Headache and neck pain overlap; CTA of the neck shows no dissection.
Sudden headache overlaps; no sellar mass or hemorrhage on CT and no visual field or ocular motor deficit.
Headache overlaps; no hyperdense sinus or venous infarct on CT, and the aneurysmal SAH explains the presentation.
Excluded by subarachnoid blood on CT.

key_clinical_evidence: Sudden, peak-in-seconds 'thunderclap' headache is SAH until proven otherwise — peak intensity ≤1 minute is the highest-yield historical feature.

Non-contrast CT is close to 100% sensitive within 6 hours of onset on a modern scanner read by an experienced radiologist; sensitivity falls after 6 hours and markedly by days 5 to 7, and anemia lowers it, so a negative CT does not exclude SAH in late presenters.

After a negative CT, lumbar puncture is indicated when the patient presents more than 6 hours after onset or has a new neurological deficit; spectrophotometric bilirubin needs about 12 hours to form and persists for about two weeks or longer.
Distinguish SAH from traumatic LP using non-clearing RBC counts across tubes 1-4 and xanthochromia (absent in traumatic).
Once SAH is confirmed, CT angiography of the head and neck characterizes the aneurysm and drives the clipping-versus-coiling decision.
Hunt-Hess and WFNS grades stratify clinical severity and outcome; modified Fisher grade predicts vasospasm risk from CT blood distribution.
Neurogenic stress cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo pattern, troponin elevation, T-wave inversions, QTc prolongation) is common in SAH and should not divert attention to a primary cardiac workup.

Nimodipine 60 mg PO every 4 hours for 21 days is the only proven pharmacologic prophylaxis for delayed cerebral ischemia in aneurysmal SAH — it does not prevent angiographic vasospasm but improves outcomes.
Securing the ruptured aneurysm by coiling or clipping as early as feasible, preferably within 24 hours of onset, reduces rebleeding, which carries high mortality.
Delayed cerebral ischemia occurs mainly between days 3 and 14; frequent neurological examination is the core of surveillance and transcranial Doppler is a reasonable adjunct.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Catecholamine surge from acute SAH causes neurogenic myocardial injury; apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis on echocardiography fits stress cardiomyopathy, and the focus remains on securing the aneurysm.
red_herrings.data_point: Troponin I 2.8 ng/mL, BNP 486 and deep T-wave inversions V1-V5 with chest pain in a man with a prior STEMI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Cardiac biomarker rise plus ST/T-wave changes may anchor the workup toward a primary acute coronary syndrome and a cardiology-first pathway.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A thunderclap headache with neck stiffness needs non-contrast CT before any antithrombotic escalation or catheterization; with SAH confirmed, antiplatelets are held and catheterization is not pursued for neurogenic troponin.
red_herrings.data_point: EMS gave an extra 325 mg of aspirin and the team considered cardiac catheterization for presumed STEMI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Invites a cardiology-first pathway with more antithrombotic therapy and catheterization before head imaging.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Lewis is a 58-year-old man with CAD on dual antiplatelet therapy who presents with simultaneous sudden onset severe headache and chest pain. He was lifting boxes at home when he experienced sudden onset of what he describes as 'the most horrible headache and chest pain at the same time.' The headache reached 10/10 within seconds. Chest pain was pressure-like, substernal, 7/10. He called 911. EMS found BP 218/128 mmHg. He was given aspirin 325 mg additional dose by EMS and was rushed to the ED for concern of STEMI. ECG in the field showed deep T-wave inversions V1-V4 leading to cardiac catheterization consideration. He is on dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) for a stent placed 2 years ago. The primary team is focused on the cardiac presentation. The neurology consult was triggered by the ER nurse who noted the headache was described as 'thunderclap' and he has neck stiffness.
